The multi-material coating design consists of 7 bilayers of SiO2/Ta2O5 in the outer layers, followed by 5 bilayers of aSi/SiO2 in the inner layers.
The multi-material coating design reduces the total number of coating layers from 38 to 26, while maintaining the same high reflectivity of ~0.5 ppm transmission.
Experimental measurements showed the multi-material coating stack can achieve an optical absorption of only (5.3 ± 0.4) ppm at 1550 nm.
The multi-material coating design can reduce Brownian thermal noise by 25% compared to standard SiO2/Ta2O5 coatings.
aSi has a significantly higher refractive index of 3.5 compared to 2.2 for Ta2O5, allowing thinner high-index layers and fewer total coating layers.
The mechanical loss of aSi is at least a factor of 10 lower than Ta2O5 at cryogenic temperatures, providing another direct reduction in coating thermal noise.
The total thickness of the multi-material coating stack is reduced from 8.684 μm to 5.701 μm, a 34% reduction.
Experimental measurements showed the SiO2/Ta2O5 coating stack had an optical absorption of (1.7 ± 0.3) ppm at 1550 nm.
The aSi/SiO2 coating stack had an optical absorption of 1035 ppm for s-polarization and 1428 ppm for p-polarization at 1550 nm and 42 degree angle of incidence.
Cryogenic operation is planned for future gravitational wave detectors like Advanced LIGO and the Einstein Telescope, in order to reduce thermal noise in the test mass mirrors.
Crystalline silicon (cSi) is planned to be used as the substrate material in future gravitational wave detectors due to its low mechanical loss at cryogenic temperatures.
The SiO2/Ta2O5 coating stack requires 18 bilayers to achieve high reflectivity, while the aSi/SiO2 stack only requires 8 bilayers.
The multi-material coating design reduces the total coating thickness by 34% compared to the standard SiO2/Ta2O5 design.
The mechanical loss of aSi decreases with decreasing temperature, leading to lower thermal noise at cryogenic temperatures compared to the SiO2/Ta2O5 stack.
The multi-material coating design places the higher-absorbing aSi layers in the lower-intensity region of the coating stack to maintain low overall optical absorption.
